title: Šta Englezi krivo kažu
theme: This mixed review walks the whole-book map without opening a new system.
reviewerNotes: Pedagogy re-audit after Fact Checker. Mixed review only. Kept Bosnian-editor aspect soft-gap (pests jesti/pojesti, try t10, quiz q1). Compressed whyHere/pattern/next slogan stacks, folded englishLies It-list, fixed pests colon, swapped se/moja vocab to Ana/Emir list heads, normalized q3 punctuation. Bosnian morphology untouched. Still draft. Final native try/quiz sweep: removed cat-plot/joke weak distractors; replaced select meta slots with named undrilled drills (Ano, za njega, Hoću, Pijte, Doći ću, tata, Nema auta, moja prijateljica); Ch11 trebati personal+acc left untouched; status draft.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you walk the whole notebook again without learning a new system. Piles, jobs, matching, doing-words, and little words already have their shelves, from coffee as she to se in second place. English will still push you toward one wrong habit from each shelf. This chapter names those habits and checks the map.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because it keeps coffee still in every job, uses it for almost every thing, lets my stay still while the noun moves, uses one eat for ongoing and finished action, and lets myself wander to the front of a sentence. Bosnian answers each lie with a different shelf from this book. The mix-up starts when you grab the wrong shelf for the headache in front of you.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you Ana’s coffee line Želim kahvu, and Chapter 12 just parked Ja se zovem Ana. Together they carry three systems you now own. Kahva is she from the pile chapter. Kahvu is the want-it job on that same she-word. Se sits in second place after Ja. Today you only rehearse those shelves side by side. You do not open a new chart.
knownLine.speaker: Ana

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: Use the map before you invent a fix, and ask which shelf is broken. Last-letter filing is piles. Moved endings for name-it, want-it, none-of-it, to-it, or with-it are jobs. My or big copying the noun is matching. Time or finished action is doing-words, including eat versus eat up. A little word that tried to open the line is second place. The whole review is one headache mapped to one shelf.

rows: He, she, leftover from the last letter
Name it, want it, none, to it, with it
My and big ride with the noun
Now, past, future, eat vs eat up
Se, mi, je, sam, ću in second place

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Five pests come back today, one from each shelf. Tata ends in a and still sits in the he pile. Želim kahva leaves coffee in the name-it form. Moja kahvu matches the pile and misses the job. Jesti and pojesti are not free twins for every eat. Open jesti covers action in progress or habit, and sealed pojesti covers finish it up. Se zovem parks the little word in first place. Name the pest, then open the right older chapter. Do not build a sixth system.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to treat every wrong ending as the same kind of mistake. Kahvu is not a pile change, not a tense, and not a matching failure. It is the want-it job on a she-word you already filed. Se zovem is not a pile problem either. It is a parking problem. If you swing one hammer at every miss, you invent grammar nobody in Sarajevo said.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester hung work on the ends of words, filed things into piles, and clustered small words early. Later English moved a lot of that work into little separate words and freer order. You speak the later version.

Bosnian kept more of the older toolkit on the word itself. That is why this notebook needed shelves instead of one mega chart. English speakers go wrong when they expect one English habit to cover five Bosnian jobs. The map is the fix. The coffee stayed the same coffee the whole time.

items.speaker: Amira
items.english: That is coffee in the she pile. Last letter a did the filing.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: I want coffee. Same she-word. The u marks the want-it job.

items.speaker: Emir
items.english: That is a bridge in the he pile. A consonant did the filing.

items.speaker: Emir
items.english: I want a bridge. He-pile things often keep the list form in the want-it job.

items.speaker: Amira
items.english: That is my coffee in the name-it job. Moja matches she-pile kahva.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: I want my coffee. Moju rides with kahvu in the want-it job.

items.speaker: Emir
items.english: I drank beer. Sam sits in second place. The past ending matches Emir.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: I drank beer. Sam is still second. The doing-word ending matches Ana.

items.speaker: Amira
items.english: I will come. Ću parks in second place after Ja.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: My name is Ana. Se sits in second place. Se zovem would fail.

items.speaker: Emir
items.english: My name is Emir. Zovem takes first place, so Ja can stay home.

items.speaker: Amira
items.english: There is no coffee. Kahve is the of-and-none job on the same she-word.

items.explanation: Last letter a puts coffee in the she pile.
Want-it job on a she-word. A becomes u.

items.prompt: Someone says Želim kahva. Which shelf broke?
items.explanation: They left coffee in the name-it form. The pile was already she.

items.prompt: Pick the matching pair for want-it coffee.
items.explanation: Matching copies both the she pile and the want-it job.

items.prompt: Se zovem Ana. Which shelf broke?
items.explanation: Se tried to open the sentence. Ja se zovem or Zovem se fixes it.

items.prompt: Pio sam pivo. Where does sam sit?
items.explanation: Pio is first. Sam is the past helper in second place.

options: Because the u is a job mark on the same she-word
items.explanation: Pile and job are different shelves. Kahva and kahvu stay she.

items.prompt: most in the want-it job is often which form?
options: mosta as the only want-it form
items.explanation: He-pile things often keep the list form in the want-it job.
Ja is first. Ću is second. Ću cannot lead.

items.prompt: You are mid-meal and eating bread. Which twin?
items.explanation: Open jesti for action in progress. Pojesti is the sealed finish-it twin from Chapter 9.

questions.question: Jesti vs pojesti. Which line finishes the food?
questions.explanation: Pojedi is the sealed command. Jedem is open and in progress. Aspect lives on the doing-words shelf.

questions.question: Želim kahvu mixes which two shelves?
questions.explanation: Kahva is she. Kahvu is the want-it form on that same she-word.

questions.question: Why does Moja kahvu fail?
options: Se needed to open the line
questions.explanation: Moju kahvu copies both pile and job. Moja kahva is the name-it pair.

questions.question: Why does Se zovem Ana fail?
questions.explanation: Little words sit in second place. Ja se zovem and Zovem se both work.

questions.question: Pio sam pivo shows which shelves together?
questions.explanation: Past marking lives on the doing-word side. Sam still parks in second place.

questions.question: tata ends in a. Which pile?
options: No pile. Kinship words skip filing.
questions.explanation: Tata is the Chapter 1 pest named again in today’s pests. Dad stays he even though the list word ends in a.

next.body: You now have the whole map in one place, from piles and jobs through matching, doing-words, and little words in second place. There is no Chapter 14 in this handbook. Go back to coffee, the bridge, and Ana when a line feels wrong, and name the shelf before you guess.
